records.name: Tocantins
records.current_summary:
Tocantins stands entirely under Brazil's nationally uniform framework: marriage equality since 2013, name and gender-marker change at the registry without surgery since 2018, homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism by the Supreme Court in 2019, and non-binary civil-registry amendments allowed by a 2025 superior-court ruling — protections built by the courts rather than statute, with repeal efforts active in Congress bearing on their stability.

No Tocantins-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement pattern is on file. A Brazilian law-firm guide records that the legal rights are identical nationwide while major cities are broadly welcoming and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction — a distinction that reaches through Tocantins as elsewhere.

Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; that national profile, not any local divergence, sets the state's risk. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing political visibility at local level nationally.

sources.claim: Country-framework page (revised through 2026): same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, last updated 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper - same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

records.name: Espirito Santo
records.current_summary: Brazil's uniform national framework applies to Espirito Santo; no state-specific law or enforcement pattern was found. ANTRA's 2025 state tally records 2 killings in the unit - a low absolute count. The dossier's key structural caveat applies here: at least 68% of killings occur outside state capitals, in interior towns, so a low state count can hide interior exposure.

sources.claim: Same-sex marriage legal nationwide since May 2013 (CNJ Resolution 175/2013, binding on all civil registries in a 14-1 vote); on 13 Jun 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines; adoption rights since 2015; LGB people serve openly in the military; explicit national discrimination protections since 2019. This is the uniform framework a visitor stands under in any Brazilian state.

2026 status: a 2019 STF ruling makes discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity federally criminal, though no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists and Congress has repeal efforts; the Superior Court of Justice (2023) allowed nonbinary people to amend civil records; intersex people lack specific protections. Framework applies uniformly across Brazil's states.

records.name: Sao Paulo
records.current_summary: Mixed picture: Sao Paulo led the national ranking in 2024 with 16 killings of travestis and trans people, then fell to 4 recorded killings in 2025 - out of the top group. The country's dominant geographic pattern applies here: at least 68% of the 2024 killings (83 of 122) happened outside state capitals, in interior cities, so the risk sits in Sao Paulo's interior rather than the capital.
records.current_localsOnly: The recorded killings are of local trans residents - the 2024 national victim profile is majority young, Black and poor - rather than visitors; the protective federal machinery (name/gender change, hate-crime doctrine) is likewise resident-facing administrative law.

records.name: Puducherry
records.current_summary:
Puducherry is a union territory with a partial legislature: recognition and welfare policy for trans people is set principally by the federal government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The framework that governs it shifted sharply in March 2026: parliament passed an amendment removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinnar) and intersex people, mandating medical certification for identity documents and for surgery; critics and a court-appointed advisory panel warn it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people, protests followed the vote in several cities, and the change bears uniformly on every state and territory.

Nationally recurring policing practice — treating trans appearance as a suspicion category in transit spaces, evidenced by an August 2024 railway-platform groping complaint (an FIR was filed and intrusive questioning reported) — reaches union-territory visitors through federal transport policing rather than any local law.
records.current_localsOnly: Welfare-board status and the documentation machinery of the 2019 Act and its 2026 amendment are resident-facing: the union-territory dependency described above bears on services and certificates for local transgender people rather than on how visitors are treated.

sources.claim: The 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill amends the 2019 law: it removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted categories and intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition - HRW calls it a major reversal of the 2014 rights and urges the president not to sign it (articles dated 26 Mar 2026).

Amendment bill approved by both houses (article 2026, awaiting presidential assent): removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court 'third gender' ruling; narrows the 2019 definition of transgender person; government says the narrower definition improves welfare delivery, critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people; mandatory medical certification described as an attack on privacy and dignity.
